one-relation.third-constant-conversion-c.formal:
Let $(V, Q)$ be a real quadratic space of signature $(p, q)$, $n = p + q \geq 2$, with events carrying a time coordinate and space coordinates measured in independently chosen units, so that a quadratic form on events is dimensionally homogeneous only after a conversion constant $c$ is chosen, $Q = c^{2}t^{2} - |\mathbf{x}|^{2}$ in the Lorentzian case. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Existence and finiteness.)} A finite invariant ratio of length to time exists if and only if $Q$ is nondegenerate and mixed, $pq \neq 0$: the null cone is that invariant ratio, preserved by every isometry, and it is nonempty exactly when the signature is mixed; dividing $Q$ by $c^{2}$ and letting $c \to \infty$ degenerates $Q$ to the rank-one form $t^{2}$, whose zero set is the simultaneity hyperplane, the Galilean case the root paper sets aside. The word \emph{speed} is reserved for the case of clause (iv). Two of the three standing hypotheses of the root paper's no-go theorem \cite[Thm.~4.2]{ButlerT1}, nondegenerate and mixed, are jointly the existence of a finite invariant ratio; the third, $n \geq 3$, is not needed here and enters only through Zeeman's theorem below.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(One number.)} The invariant ratio is a property of a hyperbolic plane, and the isometry group is transitive on the hyperbolic planes of $(V, Q)$ (Witt's extension theorem, Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-witts-extension-theorem}), so every hyperbolic plane carries the same $c$. This is the Witt fact of Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences}(1): the uniqueness of the boost qubit and the uniqueness of the invariant ratio are one statement.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Invisible in the Witt chart, fixed in the metric chart.)} On a hyperbolic plane with orthonormal pair $e_{0}, e_{1}$, $e_{0}^{2} = 1$, $e_{1}^{2} = -1$, the Witt chart $f_{\pm} = \tfrac12(e_{0} \pm e_{1})$, $f_{+} \cdot f_{-} = \tfrac12$, has a one-parameter freedom the metric chart does not show, $f_{+} \to \lambda f_{+}$, $f_{-} \to f_{-}/\lambda$, $\lambda > 0$; that rescaling is exactly the boost rotor of rapidity $\eta = \log\lambda$ acting on the orthonormal frame, $R = \cosh(\eta/2) - \sinh(\eta/2)\,e_{0}e_{1}$, with $R e_{0}\tilde{R} = \cosh\eta\, e_{0} + \sinh\eta\, e_{1}$ and $R f_{+}\tilde{R} = e^{\eta}f_{+}$, and the coordinate velocity of the boosted time axis is $c\tanh\eta$. The Witt chart contains rapidity, a dimensionless number, and no other quantity; the metric chart contains time and length separately; the transition from one to the other is what requires the conversion constant $c$. That the algebra fixes orbits and not speeds, as the entropy paper states \cite[Fact~2.2]{ButlerT8}, is this clause: the Witt chart is scale-free, and the geometric normalisation that converts rapidity to time is the chart transition.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(A speed with an arrow.)} The set $\{Q > 0\}$ retracts onto the unit sphere of the positive part and has the components of $S^{p-1}$: two when $p = 1$, one when $p \geq 2$, none when $p = 0$; symmetrically $\{Q < 0\}$ splits exactly when $q = 1$. Hence a nondegenerate form admits a future/past split, a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ of time orientation, if and only if $\min(p, q) = 1$. The dark-matter paper's causal criterion \cite[Prop.~3.1]{ButlerT14}, stated there as a definition, is thereby a theorem about the cone: a signature has a single time if and only if its timelike set is disconnected. $c$ is a speed, a length over one time, precisely in the causal signatures; in $(2,2)$ the null cone exists and determines the form, so an invariant ratio exists, but there is no single time to divide by and no arrow, and the invariant is not a speed.
\end{enumerate}
With Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-null-cone-determines-form-zeemans}, the cone determines $Q$ up to scale, so $c$ is a conformal invariant and survives every conformal step of the series, the projective-to-conformal completion, the correspondence between points and lines of conformal spinors (the twistor correspondence) and the tractor bundle, which is why those papers can set $c = 1$ with no effect on their results; $G$ does not survive the conformal step, needing the scale the conformal class forgets, and $\hbar$ does not survive the classical chart, needing the ordering. The three constants therefore sit at three levels: $c$ at the conformal level (the cone), $G$ at the metric level (the scale), $\hbar$ at the Witt level (the ordering); and the exponent matrix of $(c, \hbar, G)$ over (length, time, mass) has determinant $-2$, so the three together fix the three base units and every remaining constant is dimensionless over (length, time, mass), while $\hbar$ and $G$ alone fix no base unit. Zeeman's theorem (Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-null-cone-determines-form-zeemans}) connects (iv) back to the conformal level: in a causal signature with $n \geq 3$ the causal automorphisms are the conformal ones up to dilation.
one-relation.third-constant-conversion-c.technical:
On a real quadratic space of signature $(p,q)$ with $n = p + q \geq 2$, where time and space are measured in independent units, a finite invariant ratio of length to time exists if and only if $Q$ is nondegenerate and mixed, $pq \neq 0$: it is the null cone. Witt's extension theorem makes the isometry group transitive on hyperbolic planes, so the ratio is a single number $c$. In the Witt chart $f_{\pm} = \tfrac12(e_{0} \pm e_{1})$ the rescaling $f_{+} \to \lambda f_{+}$, $f_{-} \to f_{-}/\lambda$ is the boost of rapidity $\eta = \log\lambda$; that chart holds only rapidity, so the transition to the metric chart's separate time and length is what needs $c$.

A future/past split exists exactly when $\min(p,q) = 1$, so $c$ is a speed with an arrow only in causal signatures. Since the cone fixes $Q$ up to scale, $c$ is a conformal invariant, while $G$ needs the metric scale and $\hbar$ the Witt ordering; together $(c, \hbar, G)$ fix the three base units. No value of $c$ is derived.
one-relation.third-constant-conversion-c.lay: The speed of light can be seen as a conversion factor between units of time and units of length. This result shows such a factor exists only when spacetime mixes time-like and space-like directions, that there is only one such number, and that it is invisible in the quantum description and appears only on passing to the geometric one. It also places the three fundamental constants at three different levels of structure, without deriving any of their values.

proofs.main: (i) The null cone is $\{Q = 0\}$, preserved by isometries by definition; it contains a nonzero vector iff $pq \neq 0$ (the root paper's null-locus criterion, Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-null-cone-determines-form-zeemans}); the script checks that $Q/c^{2} = \mathrm{diag}(1, -c^{-2}, -c^{-2}, -c^{-2})$ has signature $(1,3)$ at $c = 1, 10, 1000$ and that at $c = \infty$ the form is $\mathrm{diag}(1, 0, 0, 0)$, of rank one with radical the simultaneity hyperplane. (ii) is Witt's extension theorem (Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-witts-extension-theorem}), which the dark-matter paper imports and Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences} uses: two hyperbolic planes are isometric, so the isometry between them extends to an isometry of $(V, Q)$. The script takes three rational null pairs of $(1,3)$, $n \cdot m = -1$, spanning three pairwise distinct hyperbolic planes, and computes that their anisotropic complements all have signature $(0,2)$, the witness the theorem needs; the theorem itself is imported. (iii) The rotor, the exponential of a boost bivector (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}), has its identities computed exactly in $\Cl(1,1)$ at $\lambda = e^{\eta} = 4$, $\cosh\eta = \tfrac{17}{8}$, $\sinh\eta = \tfrac{15}{8}$: $R\tilde{R} = 1$, $Re_{0}\tilde{R} = \cosh\eta\,e_{0} + \sinh\eta\,e_{1}$ with norms preserved, $Rf_{\pm}\tilde{R} = \lambda^{\pm 1}f_{\pm}$, the null lines the fixed lines of every boost, and the velocity $\tanh\eta = (\lambda^{2} - 1)/(\lambda^{2} + 1) = \tfrac{15}{17}$; the sign convention matters, the opposite sign in the rotor reversing the boost, and the script fixes it as stated. (iv) The retraction $(a, b) \mapsto (a, tb)$, $t \in [0, 1]$, on $\{Q > 0\}$ written as $|a|^{2} - |b|^{2} > 0$ in an orthonormal basis, deformation-retracts it onto $\{|a| = 1, b = 0\} \cong S^{p-1}$; $S^{0}$ has two components, $S^{k}$ for $k \geq 1$ one, and $S^{-1}$ is empty. The script checks the component counts on sample points: on the signatures $(1,0)$ to $(3,2)$ and $(0,3)$ it counts the classes of a union-find over rational sample points of $\{Q > 0\}$ joined by exact segments with certified $Q$-minima, compares the count with the $S^{p-1}$ count entered as a literal, certifies two classes as distinct by the sign of the time coordinate, and checks the disjunction against $\min(p, q) = 1$ on seven signatures up to $n = 5$; the proof of the count is the retraction above, not the script; the cone-determines-form clause of Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-null-cone-determines-form-zeemans} is also checked, on the signatures up to $(3,3)$, as the one-dimensionality of the space of symmetric forms vanishing on the rational null vectors. The exponent determinant is arithmetic the script performs, together with the statement that no monomial in $\hbar$ and $G$ alone has the dimension of a length, a time, or a mass. Nothing here derives a value for $c$: its number is a unit convention, and in the Planck system all three are; the only derivable things are dimensionless ratios, which the capstone examines.

one-relation.two-capacities-three-conseq.formal:
Let $(V,Q)$ be real, nondegenerate, of signature $(p,q)$, $d = p+q$. The quantum presentation of Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-presentations} supports two mode counts, which differ in general and must not be conflated:
\[
r_{\R}(p,q) = \min(p,q), \qquad r_{\C}(p,q) = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor,
\]
the \emph{real capacity}, the number of modes realisable by real null vectors (Fact \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}), and the \emph{complex capacity}, the maximal isotropic dimension of $V_{\C}$, the number of modes of the complexified reading. They agree exactly when $|p - q| \leq 1$, in particular on the split signatures $(k,k)$; for $(1,3)$ they are $1$ and $2$, for $(2,4)$ they are $2$ and $3$. Three consequences, each labelled with the capacity it uses.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(The boost qubit; real.)} $r_{\R}(1,3) = 1$: Lorentzian signature has one real hyperbolic plane, unique up to an isometry of the whole space (all such planes are conjugate under $O(1,3)$), and the anisotropic complement is definite, so pre-ascent spacetime natively supports exactly one \emph{real} quantum mode, the boost qubit. The complex capacity is two, which is the Dirac spinor of $\Cl(1,3)_{\C}$ as a two-mode Fock space of dimension $2^{2} = 4$. This clause counts the modes of $(1,3)$ and says nothing about the single-mode thermality theorem, whose mode is the ladder pair of the ascent and is counted by neither $r_{\R}(1,3)$ nor $r_{\C}(1,3)$; what is said about that theorem is a reading, Proposition \claimref{one-relation.overlap-table-sorted}(iii).
\item \emph{(Transport is capacity increment; both capacities.)} Each $(1,1)$ ascent adjoins one hyperbolic plane, hence one real null pair, hence one mode in either count: $r_{\R}$ and $r_{\C}$ each rise by exactly one per rung. The transport principle is capacity increment, and the tower's one-qubit-per-rung ladder (Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-completion-ladder}) is its restatement.
\item \emph{(The ascended capacity is three; complex.)} $r_{\C}(2,4) = 3$: the complexified ascended $\C^{6}$ has maximal isotropic dimension three, which is the Standard-Model paper's pair count $(n+2)/2$ at spacetime dimension $n = 4$, the ambient signature being $(2,n)$, so that $d = n + 2$ and, for $n$ even, $\lfloor d/2 \rfloor = (n+2)/2$ \cite[Lem.~2.12]{ButlerT12}. Under that count the Standard-Model paper selects the strong force and four dimensions, on the two conditionalities it declares \cite[Prop.~4.3]{ButlerT12}. The real capacity of the ascended space is two: its third pair lies in the complexification, as the dark-matter paper's flag Fact records \cite[Fact~2.9]{ButlerT14}.
\end{enumerate}
Which capacity a physical count uses is therefore a statement to be made each time, not a residue: (1) is real, (3) is complex, (2) holds for both capacities. The successor problem is which of the two the state of the section “Spacetime as the manifold of vacuum lines” selects.
one-relation.two-capacities-three-conseq.technical:
For a real nondegenerate signature $(p,q)$, $d = p + q$, the quantum reading supports two mode counts: the real capacity $r_{\R}(p,q) = \min(p,q)$, counting modes realised by real null vectors, and the complex capacity $r_{\C}(p,q) = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$, the maximal isotropic dimension of $V_{\C}$. They agree exactly when $|p - q| \leq 1$; for $(1,3)$ they are $1$ and $2$, for $(2,4)$ they are $2$ and $3$.

Consequences: (1) Lorentzian spacetime has one real mode, the boost qubit, unique up to isometry, while the complex count two is the Dirac spinor as a two-mode Fock space. (2) Each $(1,1)$ ascent raises both capacities by exactly one. (3) $r_{\C}(2,4) = 3$, the Standard-Model pair count at spacetime dimension four, while the real capacity there is two. Which capacity a physical count uses must be stated each time.
one-relation.two-capacities-three-conseq.lay: Reading spacetime geometry as a system of fermion modes, there are two ways to count the modes: using only real directions, or allowing complex ones. The two counts usually differ, and for ordinary spacetime they give one and two. Each step up the tower of extended spaces adds exactly one mode to both counts, and the complex count of the extended six-dimensional space is three.

proofs.main: The real count is Fact \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity}. For the complex count (the modes of the Witt reading of \claimref{one-relation.two-presentations}): a totally isotropic $U \subset V_{\C}$ satisfies $U \subseteq U^{\perp}$, and nondegeneracy gives $\dim U + \dim U^{\perp} = d$, so $2\dim U \leq d$; the bound is attained by the null spans of $\lfloor d/2 \rfloor$ pairs, built from the real hyperbolic planes together with pairs $(e + ie')/2$, $-(e - ie')/2$ on each two-dimensional block of the anisotropic kernel, whose square $\{c(e+ie'), c(e+ie')\} = 2(Q(e) - Q(e')) = 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}) vanishes because the kernel is definite and its diagonal entries equal. Both counts are exhibited by the script on $(1,1)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,4)$: the pairs are written down and every anticommutator computed. (1) $\min(1,3) = 1$; the anisotropic complement of the boost plane is the negative-definite $(e_{2}, e_{3})$ block of the Witt decomposition (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-decomposition}), on which the script confirms $Q(ae_{2} + be_{3}) = -(a^{2} + b^{2}) < 0$ for rational $(a,b) \neq 0$, so no null vector lies in the anisotropic complement and no second anticommuting real pair exists; the Witt decomposition is unique up to isometry by Witt's extension theorem (Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-witts-extension-theorem}), which is the sense in which the boost plane is unique, and the same Witt fact is the uniqueness of the invariant ratio (Lemma \claimref{one-relation.third-constant-conversion-constant-between-charts}(ii)). The agreement locus: for $p \leq q$, $r_{\R} = p$ and $r_{\C} = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor = \lfloor (p+q)/2 \rfloor$, so $r_{\R} = r_{\C}$ if and only if $2p \leq p + q \leq 2p + 1$, that is $0 \leq q - p \leq 1$, and symmetrically for $q \leq p$; the script's grid check illustrates this. (2) $\min(p+1,q+1) = \min(p,q) + 1$ and $\lfloor (d+2)/2 \rfloor = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor + 1$, arithmetic identities, recorded by the script on the grid $p, q \leq 8$. (3) $\lfloor 6/2 \rfloor = 3$ and $\min(2,4) = 2$, with the three pairs of $\Cl(2,4)_{\C}$ exhibited, two real and one complex.

one-relation.two-presentations.formal:
The defining relation of a Clifford algebra, $\{e_{a}, e_{b}\} = 2g_{ab}\mathbf{1}$, carries both theories as its two canonical presentations. On an orthogonal basis the relation displays a metric: the geometric reading, which the geometry paper carries to the vacuum Einstein equations and proves there equivalent to parallelism of the scale tractor \cite[Thm.~4.5]{ButlerT6}. On a Witt basis, a maximal isotropic decomposition $V_{\C} = W \oplus \bar{W}$ with the cross pairing normalised to $\ip{w_{i}}{\bar{w}_{j}} = \tfrac12\delta_{ij}$, the same relation reads
\[
\{c(w_{i}), c(w_{j})\} = 0, \qquad \{c(w_{i}), c(\bar{w}_{j})\} = \delta_{ij},
\]
verbatim the canonical anticommutation relations of $\dim W$ fermionic modes, with the Fock module supplied by the pure-spinor construction (Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-pure-spinors-incidence-chart}). Over $\R$ the same reading is available on the real null pairs alone, and Fact \claimref{tower.witt-index-quantum-capacity} counts them. The metric is the anticommutator and the anticommutator is the metric; geometric versus quantum is a choice of chart on one object, not a choice of object. The claim is kinematic: it identifies the metric datum with the CAR algebra, and says nothing about dynamics, states, and measurement, which carry their own levels below.
one-relation.two-presentations.technical:
The Clifford relation $\{e_{a}, e_{b}\} = 2g_{ab}\mathbf{1}$ has two canonical presentations. On an orthogonal basis it displays a metric, the geometric reading. On a Witt basis $V_{\C} = W \oplus \bar{W}$ with $\ip{w_{i}}{\bar{w}_{j}} = \tfrac12\delta_{ij}$ it reads $\{c(w_{i}), c(w_{j})\} = 0$ and $\{c(w_{i}), c(\bar{w}_{j})\} = \delta_{ij}$, the canonical anticommutation relations of $\dim W$ fermionic modes, with the Fock module supplied by the pure-spinor construction.

Both bases generate the same algebra, so geometric versus quantum is a choice of chart on one object. The claim is kinematic only: it identifies the metric datum with the CAR algebra and says nothing about dynamics, states or measurement.
one-relation.two-presentations.lay: The basic rule of a Clifford algebra can be written in two ways. In one it describes distances and angles, the language of geometry and gravity; in the other it is exactly the rule obeyed by fermions, the language of quantum theory. The paper takes this to mean that geometry and quantum structure are two views of one object, though only at the level of structure, not of how things evolve.

proofs.main: The orthogonal reading is definitional. For the Witt reading, let $V_{\C} = W \oplus \bar{W}$ be a maximal isotropic decomposition with the cross pairing normalised as stated (a dual basis of $\bar{W}$ exists because the form is nondegenerate and $W$ is isotropic, so $\ip{w_{i}}{\cdot}$ restricted to $\bar{W}$ are independent functionals). For $w_{i}, w_{j} \in W$ isotropy gives $g(w_{i}, w_{j}) = 0$, so $\{c(w_{i}), c(w_{j})\} = 2g(w_{i}, w_{j}) = 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}) (with $c$ the action on the Fock module of \claimref{one-relation.imported-pure-spinors-incidence-chart}), likewise on $\bar{W}$; for the cross terms the normalised pairing gives $\{c(w_{i}), c(\bar{w}_{j})\} = 2g(w_{i}, \bar{w}_{j}) = \delta_{ij}$, the CAR of a Witt basis (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}). Both bases generate the same algebra, since a Witt basis is a linear change of basis of an orthogonal one over $\C$. The script exhibits the bases explicitly: the real null pair of $\Cl(1,1)$; for $\Cl(1,3)_{\C}$ the real pair $(e_{0} \pm e_{1})/2$ on the boost plane and the complex pair $(e_{2} + ie_{3})/2$, $-(e_{2} - ie_{3})/2$ on the anisotropic kernel; for $\Cl(2,4)_{\C}$ two real pairs and one complex pair; and verifies every anticommutator and the invertibility of the change of basis over the Gaussian rationals.

one-relation.vector-derivative-covariant.formal:
Let $D = A^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$ be a first-order operator with constant coefficients $A^{\mu} \in \Cl(1,3)$ acting by left multiplication on $\Cl(1,3)$-valued fields on Minkowski space (hence on every minimal left ideal), and suppose $D$ is covariant under the spin group: $D(R\,\psi\circ\Lambda_{R}^{-1}) = R\,(D\psi)\circ\Lambda_{R}^{-1}$ for every rotor $R \in \mathrm{Spin}^{+}(1,3)$, $\Lambda_{R}$ its vector transformation. Then $A^{\mu} = \gamma^{\mu}(a + bI)$ for real $a, b$, with $I = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$ the pseudoscalar: $D = (a - bI)
abla$ for the vector derivative $
abla = \gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$, and $a - bI$ is invertible whenever $(a,b) 
eq (0,0)$. Among covariant constant-coefficient first-order operators acting by left multiplication, the vector derivative is unique up to an invertible constant factor. (Right multiplications are outside the class: $\psi \mapsto 
abla\psi\,B$ for constant $B$ is covariant, and is not of the form $A^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$ acting on the left unless $B$ is central.)
one-relation.vector-derivative-covariant.technical:
Let $D = A^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$ have constant coefficients $A^{\mu} \in \Cl(1,3)$ acting by left multiplication on $\Cl(1,3)$-valued fields on Minkowski space, and suppose it is covariant under every rotor of $\mathrm{Spin}^{+}(1,3)$. Then $A^{\mu} = \gamma^{\mu}(a + bI)$ with $a, b$ real, so $D = (a - bI)
abla$ with $
abla = \gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$, and $a - bI$ is invertible unless $a = b = 0$.

So within this class the vector derivative is unique up to an invertible constant factor. Right multiplications $\psi \mapsto 
abla\psi\, B$ are covariant but lie outside the class unless $B$ is central.
one-relation.vector-derivative-covariant.lay: Relativity requires a law to look the same to all observers. Among the simplest kinds of first-order derivative operator in the spacetime algebra, only one meets that requirement, up to a constant multiple: the vector derivative. So, within that class, the operator in the electron's equation is not a free choice.

pairing.imported-stabiliser-tangent.formal:
On the Fock space of $
u \geq 2$ boundary modes the bivectors of $\so(2
u)$ split as hops $a_i^{\dagger}a_j$ (with the Cartan elements $a_i^{\dagger}a_i - 	frac12$), pair annihilations $a_ia_j$ and pair creations $a_i^{\dagger}a_j^{\dagger}$. On the vacuum every hop with $i 
eq j$ and every annihilation vanishes and every Cartan element is a scalar, so hops and annihilations are the stabiliser of the vacuum ray; the creations span the tangent of the orbit of Witt vacua, of dimension $
u(
u-1)/2$. A hop rotation fixes the vacuum, a pairing rotation moves it, and the necessity witness of the singularity paper's envelope corollary, $\ket{00} \mapsto 	frac35\ket{00} + 	frac45\ket{11}$, is the pairing rotation on one pair at $(\cos	heta, \sin	heta) = (	frac35, 	frac45)$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Prop.~13.4, Cor.~11.6]{ButlerT5}; the orbit is the spinor variety of \cite{Cartan1938, Chevalley1954}, imported there, and the exponential form of a rotated vacuum is Thouless's \cite{Thouless1960}, imported by the laboratory paper \cite[Fact~2.10]{ButlerT16}.

eq j$ and annihilations kill the vacuum and Cartan elements act as scalars, so these form the stabiliser of the vacuum ray, while the creations span the tangent to the orbit of Witt vacua, of dimension $
u(
u-1)/2$.

A hop rotation fixes the vacuum and a pairing rotation moves it; the witness $\ket{00} \mapsto 	frac35\ket{00} + 	frac45\ket{11}$ is the pairing rotation on one pair. The fact restates series results; the orbit is the classical spinor variety and a rotated vacuum has the Thouless exponential form.
pairing.imported-stabiliser-tangent.lay: In a system of two or more fermion modes, the basic symmetry operations come in three kinds: moving a particle from one mode to another, removing a pair, and creating a pair. On the empty state the first two leave its direction unchanged, while creating pairs genuinely moves it. So, to first order, the ways the vacuum can be changed are exactly the pair creations.

pairing.imported-two-readings-capacities.formal:
The relation $\{e_a, e_b\} = 2g_{ab}$ on a Witt basis is the canonical anticommutation relations, the Fock module being supplied by the pure-spinor construction. A real quadratic space of signature $(p,q)$ has real capacity $\min(p,q)$ and complex capacity $\lfloor (p+q)/2 floor$; for $(1,3)$ these are one and two, the complex reading being the Dirac spinor as a two-mode Fock space. A vacuum at a point of spacetime is an extra datum, a null direction at the point, which the reading must supply. Every Weyl spinor of $\mathrm{Spin}(2
u, \C)$ is pure for $2
u \leq 6$, so at $
u = 2$ and $
u = 3$ every parity-definite state is the vacuum of some Witt decomposition. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Props.~3.1, 3.2, 4.1(3), Fact~2.10]{ButlerT16}; the capacity count is \cite[Thm.~4.3]{ButlerT3}.

pred.gravity-entangles-standard-phase.technical:
Registered prediction (registered 2026-10-09; reading chosen 2026-10-12, third addendum). Under the element reading of the frozen-point connection's equations, and under premises P-i to P-vi, held fixed before any result (P-ii is unitary evolution), two masses $m_A$ and $m_B$, each held in a superposition of two places, become entangled by the standard phase

with $r_{ij}$ the distance between branch $i$ of the first mass and branch $j$ of the second.

rungs.imported-fock-representation-bogol.formal: For a complex Hermitian space $E$ of dimension $n$, the Fock space $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ is the irreducible spinor module of the complex Clifford algebra on $2n$ generators, its parity grading the chirality decomposition; the orthogonal transformations of the $2n$ Majorana generators preserving the canonical anticommutation relations form the compact $O(2n)$, implemented by $\mathrm{Pin}(2n)$, with $SO(2n)$ implemented by $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$; those preserving the complex structure form $U(n)$, acting as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(g)$ up to a determinant phase. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Fact~2.11]{ButlerT12}; \cite[Lecture~20]{FultonHarris1991}; \cite[Ch.~I, \S\S 2, 5]{LawsonMichelsohn1989}.

The orthogonal transformations of the $2n$ Majorana generators, which preserve the canonical anticommutation relations, form $O(2n)$, implemented by $\mathrm{Pin}(2n)$, with $SO(2n)$ implemented by $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$; those preserving the complex structure form $U(n)$, acting as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(g)$ up to a determinant phase.

standard-model.imported-fock-representat.formal: Let $E$ be a complex vector space of dimension $n$ with a Hermitian inner product, and let $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ be the Fock space of $n$ fermionic modes, with creation operators the exterior multiplications and annihilation operators the contractions. The $2n$ Majorana combinations of these operators generate an action of the complex Clifford algebra of a $2n$-dimensional orthogonal space on $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$, which is its irreducible spinor module; the parity grading $\Lambda^{\mathrm{even}} \oplus \Lambda^{\mathrm{odd}}$ is the chirality decomposition into the two half-spinor modules. The orthogonal transformations of the Majorana generators preserve the canonical anticommutation relations and are implemented on $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ by the group $\mathrm{Pin}(2n)$, the connected component $SO(2n)$ by $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$, which acts on each half-spinor module irreducibly for $n \ge 2$; the transformations preserving the complex structure of $E$, equivalently the mode number, form $U(n) \subset SO(2n)$, acting on $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(g)$ up to a determinant phase. For $n = 3$ this is the structure of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-pair-systems-two-chirality-halves}; for $n = 5$ it is $\Lambda^{\bullet}\C^{5}$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Lecture~20, \S 20.1]{FultonHarris1991} for the spinor module as an exterior algebra and its half-spin decomposition; \cite[Ch.~I, \S\S 2, 5]{LawsonMichelsohn1989} for $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$ as the double cover of $SO(2n)$ and its spin representation; the Fock-space form is the standard second-quantised reading of the same construction.
standard-model.imported-fock-representat.technical:
Let $E$ be an $n$-dimensional complex Hermitian space and $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ the Fock space of $n$ fermionic modes, with creation by exterior multiplication and annihilation by contraction. The $2n$ Majorana combinations generate the complex Clifford algebra of a $2n$-dimensional orthogonal space, and $\Lambda^{\bullet}E$ is its irreducible spinor module, with $\Lambda^{\mathrm{even}} \oplus \Lambda^{\mathrm{odd}}$ the two half-spinor modules.

The orthogonal transformations of the generators are implemented by $\mathrm{Pin}(2n)$, and $SO(2n)$ by $\mathrm{Spin}(2n)$, irreducible on each half for $n \geq 2$; the mode-number-preserving ones form $U(n) \subset SO(2n)$, acting as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(g)$ up to a determinant phase. For $n = 3$ this is the pair-system structure used in the Standard-Model analysis, and for $n = 5$ it is $\Lambda^{\bullet}\C^{5}$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$. The result is imported from Fulton and Harris and from Lawson and Michelsohn.
standard-model.imported-fock-representat.lay: The possible states of a collection of fermions, particles like electrons that cannot share a state, can be organised as the spinor representation of a Clifford algebra. The transformations that preserve the rules fermions obey form a rotation group, and those that also keep the number of particles fixed form a unitary group. This is a standard textbook result that the series imports.

synthesis.boost-stationary-incidence-vac.formal:
Use the setting of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-real-capacity}: $\Cl(2,4)$ on its Fock module with the positive Hermitian structure $g^{*} = g^{-1}$ for every generator, which is not $\Spin(2,4)$-invariant (clause (iv) of that theorem: boosts, translations and dilations are not unitary for it, so the units and the origin are fixed by it; under the invariant twistor form of signature $(2,2)$ the lines of real points are null and carry no states, filed alongside, synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-the-real-slice), the ascent mode $a = \nO$ with $N = a^{*}a$, the boost qubit $b$, the spectator $c$, a point $x = t e_{1} + r e_{2}$ with $u = t - r$, $v = t + r$, $Q(x) = uv$, the incidence line $L_{x}$ (the kernel of $X(x)$ on one chirality half), and its spanning vacua $\Omega_{x} = (1 - u\,a^{*}b^{*})\ket{0}_{+}$, $\Psi_{x} = (b^{*} - v\,a^{*})\ket{0}_{-}$. Put $f(s) = s/(1+s)$ and let $S_{\lambda} = \exp(\lambda e_{1}e_{2}/2)$ be the boost of the $(t,r)$ plane.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Boosts move lines and fix the ascent mode.)} $S_{\lambda}$ commutes with $N$, is not unitary for the Hermitian structure, and $S_{\lambda}X(x)S_{\lambda}^{-1} = X(x_{\lambda})$, where $x_{\lambda}$ has null coordinates $e^{\lambda}u$ and $e^{-\lambda}v$; so $S_{\lambda}$ maps $L_{x}$ onto $L_{x_{\lambda}}$, and the ascent occupation is one observable along the whole boost orbit $\{x_{\lambda}\}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Occupation on the line.)} For $\phi = \lambda_{1}\Omega_{x} + \mu\Psi_{x}$, $\langle N\rangle_{\phi} = \dfrac{|\lambda_{1}|^{2}u^{2} + |\mu|^{2}v^{2}}{|\lambda_{1}|^{2}(1 + u^{2}) + |\mu|^{2}(1 + v^{2})}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Boost-constancy fixes the marginal.)} The intersection, over the boost orbit of $x$, of the occupation segments $[\min, \max]\{f(u_{\lambda}^{2}), f(v_{\lambda}^{2})\}$ is the single value $f(|Q(x)|)$. Hence a section $x \mapsto \phi_{x} \in L_{x}$ whose ascent marginal is constant along every boost orbit has, at every $x$, the Gibbs marginal with $e^{-\beta(x)} = |Q(x)|$ (the ascent vacuum on the light cone $Q = 0$); such sections exist.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Boost-constancy uses the spectator.)} If $|u| \ne |v|$, the vacua on $L_{x}$ with $\langle N\rangle = f(|Q(x)|)$ are exactly $\lambda_{1}\Omega_{x} + \mu\Psi_{x}$ with $|\lambda_{1}|^{2}|u| = |\mu|^{2}|v|$; each has $\lambda_{1}\mu \ne 0$, so its $(a,b)$ state is mixed, of purity $(w_{1}^{2} + w_{2}^{2})/(w_{1} + w_{2})^{2}$ with $w_{1} = |v|(1 + u^{2})$, $w_{2} = |u|(1 + v^{2})$, and the ascent mode is purified by the boost qubit and the complex-only spectator jointly. Only at the points $|u| = |v|$ ($t = 0$ or $r = 0$), one on each orbit off the light cone, may a boost-constant section be pure on $(a,b)$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Where $2\pi$ sits.)} On a boost-constant section $\beta(x) = -\ln|Q(x)|$, in the units and about the origin the Hermitian structure fixes, so $\beta = 2\pi$ holds exactly on the hyperboloid $|Q(x)| = e^{-2\pi}$, and no boost-constant section has the same $\beta$ on two orbits with different $|Q|$.
\end{enumerate}
So a reading of the incidence vacua whose ascent marginal is constant along boost orbits (in analogy with, not an instance of, the stationarity of the Unruh state, since the boost is not unitary here) reads both capacities at once: its thermal content sits on the real hyperbolic planes and its purification on the real pair together with the complex-only spectator. Its inverse temperature is a function of the Lorentz interval, not a constant rapidity period.
synthesis.boost-stationary-incidence-vac.technical: Under the positive Hermitian structure, for which the boost is not unitary, the boost of the $(t,r)$ plane commutes with the ascent number operator and carries each incidence line to the line of the boosted point, rescaling the null coordinates oppositely. Along a boost orbit the product $uv$ is fixed, so the occupation segment $[f(u^{2}), f(v^{2})]$ at each point always contains $f(|uv|)$, and it collapses to that value where $|u| = |v|$. A section whose ascent marginal is constant along the orbits therefore has ascent Boltzmann factor $|Q(x)|$, the Lorentz interval in the units and about the origin that the Hermitian structure fixes. The vacua achieving it superpose the two spanning thermofield doubles with weights $|\lambda_1|^2 |u| = |\mu|^2 |v|$, which entangles the real pair with the complex-only spectator except on $t = 0$ or $r = 0$. The inverse temperature $-\ln|Q|$ equals $2\pi$ on one hyperboloid only.
synthesis.boost-stationary-incidence-vac.lay: At each point of spacetime the series has a line of candidate vacuum states, and some of them look thermal to the extra mode of the conformal model. Asking that this thermal reading not change as one moves along the paths a uniformly accelerating observer follows picks out a definite family. Its temperature depends only on the spacetime interval from the origin, in the units and about the origin that the construction fixes, and it needs both kinds of mode the algebra has, the real ones and the one that exists only with complex numbers.

synthesis.de-sitter-field-fixes-the-obse.technical: The tube point that a boost-KMS state reads was known up to one scale, the distance $\rho$ of the observer from the bifurcation plane, with two candidates on record: the frozen point, $\rho^{2} = 12/\Lambda$, and the surface-gravity normalisation $\rho = 1/\kappa$, which disagreed by a factor $2$ in chart length. This result computes all of them in the de Sitter gravitational field, a pure dilation of the flat background in which the boost of a plane through the scale's centre is a symmetry. The field's symmetries that commute with the boost are the boost and a rotation algebra of the bifurcation plane; on the half space of compatible tube points they fix exactly the points over the centre at $\rho^{2} = 12/\Lambda$, where the real part of the tube point's null vector is $6/\Lambda$ times the frozen point and the complexified Stelle-West vector, normalised by the scale at the tube point, is purely imaginary. On the observer of that tube point the boost generator has its largest physical norm, exactly $1/\kappa$, and the observer is in free fall; the bifurcation plane is a round sphere whose equator is there. So, with $1/\kappa$ read as the physical norm of the boost generator, the two candidates are one point; in chart length the selected scale is $2/\kappa$, and the factor $2$ is the local scale factor $\sigma = 2$ of the field at that observer. Read as a chart length, $\rho = 1/\kappa$ picks no distinguished observer. The coincidence belongs to a field with one horizon: in the Schwarzschild-de Sitter field the two horizons of one static region have different surface gravities, and the candidates separate. With no gravitational field, or a negative $\Lambda$, nothing fixes a tube point and the scale stays free, as dilation symmetry requires. Which principle makes the state's tube point respect the field's symmetries is argued, not proved: the de Sitter-invariant Hadamard state of a massive scalar is unique (Allen's theorem), and a covariant rule must then return the fixed point; the series' boundary modes are fermionic (CAR), outside that theorem's hypotheses. That rule is adopted as a costed clause (\claimref{synthesis.tube-point-clause-invariant-under-boost-commuting-symmetries}), which carries that hypothesis gap and decides fields with one horizon only.
synthesis.de-sitter-field-fixes-the-obse.lay: A state of the quantum vacuum, read near a horizon, has to pick a reference point off the real world, an imaginary-time partner of one particular observer. Earlier results showed that this choice is fixed except for one number, how far the observer stands from the horizon's edge, and two proposals for that number disagreed by a factor of two. In a universe with a positive cosmological constant both proposals, and a third one based on the horizon's own sphere, turn out to pick the same observer: the one who falls freely and sees the coldest horizon. The factor of two remains between distances measured on the flat background, and it is exactly the stretching of lengths by the gravitational field at that observer. With two horizons, as around a black hole in such a universe, the proposals part again. Without a cosmological constant nothing picks the distance. That a state's reference point is the one these symmetries pick is an adopted rule, assumed rather than derived.

synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-re.formal:
Let $\Cl(2,4)$ act on its eight-dimensional Fock module, with ground generators $e_{1}$ ($e_{1}^{2} = 1$) and $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ (squares $-1$), and ascent plane $e_{+}, e_{-}$ ($e_{\pm}^{2} = \pm 1$); give the module the Hermitian structure for which every generator is unitary, $g^{*} = g^{-1}$, which fixes the frame $e_{1}$ and the normalisation of the ascent pair. Put $
O = 	frac12(e_{+} + e_{-})$, $
inf = e_{+} - e_{-}$, the ascent mode $a = 
O$, $a^{*} = 	frac12
inf$, $N = a^{*}a$. For a point $x = t e_{1} + r e_{2}$ (every point after a spatial rotation, which is unitary and fixes $N$) put $b = 	frac12(e_{1} + e_{2})$, $b^{*} = 	frac12(e_{1} - e_{2})$, the boost-qubit mode of the $(t,r)$ plane, $c = 	frac12(e_{3} + ie_{4})$, the complex-only (spectator) mode, the null coordinates $u = t - r$, $v = t + r$, and $X(x) = 
O + x - 	frac12 Q(x)
inf$ with $Q(x) = uv$, as in Proposition \claimref{one-relation.spacetime-manifold-vacuum-lines}.

\item[(i)] \emph{(Real states fill only the real capacity.)} Call a state $\omega$ on $\Cl(p,q)_{\C}$ real if $\omega(y) \in \R$ for every $y \in \Cl(p,q)$. Then $\omega(gh) = 0$ for orthogonal generators $g, h$ of equal square, so every mode $	frac12(g + ih)$ of a definite block has occupation exactly $	frac12$; and $\{y \in V_{\C} : \omega(y^{*}y) = 0\}$ is the complexification of a real totally isotropic subspace, of dimension at most $\min(p,q)$. Hence a real state is the Fock vacuum of a maximal isotropic subspace of $V_{\C}$ only if $|p - q| \le 1$: no vacuum of the incidence chart of Fact \claimref{one-relation.imported-pure-spinors-incidence-chart} is a real state.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The two distinguished vacua of a line.)} Let $\ket{0}_{\pm}$ be the vacua of $a$ and $b$ in the two chirality halves; they differ in the occupation of $c$. The incidence line $L_{x}$ is spanned by the two vacua of definite spectator occupation
\[
\Omega_{x} = (1 - u\,a^{*}b^{*})\ket{0}_{+}, \qquad \Psi_{x} = (b^{*} - v\,a^{*})\ket{0}_{-} .
\]
On each, the state of the $(a,b)$ pair is pure, the spectator is pure and carries all the non-reality required by (i) (value $\pm i$ on $e_{3}e_{4}$), and the state is real on the subalgebra generated by $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{+}, e_{-}$. For $u 
e 0$, $\Omega_{x}$ is the thermofield double of the ascent mode's Gibbs state with $e^{- eta} = u^{2}$, with partner the boost qubit $b$ (Theorem \claimref{state-selection.partner-purification-are-canonical}); for $v 
e 0$, $\Psi_{x}$ is likewise the thermofield double at $e^{- eta} = v^{2}$, after a unitary on the partner. The inverse temperature is negative when $|u| > 1$ (respectively $|v| > 1$), the occupation then exceeding $	frac12$. At $u = 0$, $\Omega_{x}$ is the bare vacuum, not faithful on the ascent mode, and is no thermofield double (likewise $\Psi_{x}$ at $v = 0$).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(A general vacuum on the line.)} Every vacuum on $L_{x}$ has a diagonal ascent-mode marginal, of the descended Gibbs form when the ascent mode has nonzero weight (Theorem \claimref{singularity.descended-form-state-independent}; at zero weight a diagonal marginal is Gibbs only at occupation $	frac12$), with occupation $\langle N angle$ in the closed segment between $u^{2}/(1 + u^{2})$ and $v^{2}/(1 + v^{2})$, every value attained. A vacuum $\lambda\Omega_{x} + \mu\Psi_{x}$ with $\lambda\mu 
e 0$ entangles the $(a,b)$ pair with the spectator $c$: its $(a,b)$ state is mixed, and the ascent mode is purified by $b$ and $c$ jointly, not by the boost qubit alone.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Pointwise compatibility.)} So the incidence-line structure admits, at the point $x$, a vacuum with thermal ascent marginal at every inverse temperature corresponding to the segment of (iii); $ eta = 2\pi$ is attained on $L_{x}$ exactly when $e^{-\pi}$ lies between $|u|$ and $|v|$, a condition that depends on the frame and scale fixed by the Hermitian structure, the dilation not being unitary for it. At the origin every vacuum on $L_{0}$ is the ascent vacuum. Nothing here connects these vacua to the selected (descended) state of the boundary modes.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The sign of an adjoined generator.)} Let two adjoined orthogonal generators $\varepsilon$, $
u$ have $\varepsilon^{2} = -1$. Their plane is hyperbolic if and only if $
u^{2} = +1$; if $
u^{2} = -1$, every state real on the subalgebra of that plane gives its mode occupation exactly $	frac12$, by the argument of (i). A state real on the adjoined plane's subalgebra with a non-tracial ($ eta

synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-re.technical: A state that takes real values on the real Clifford algebra can only hold modes made from real null vectors, so it can be pure on at most as many modes as the real capacity; on the modes that exist only after complexification it sits at occupation one half. The incidence vacua, which are pure on three complex modes, are therefore never real. Computing them at a point with null coordinates $u$ and $v$ shows how the line is built. It is spanned by two distinguished vacua, those in which the complex-only spectator mode has definite occupation: one is a two-mode squeezed state of the ascent mode with spacetime's boost qubit, with amplitude $u$, the other a single shared excitation with amplitude $v$. Each is pure on the two real modes, real there, and is the thermofield double of a Gibbs state of the ascent mode with Boltzmann factor $u^{2}$ or $v^{2}$ (negative temperature when the factor exceeds one), with the boost qubit as partner; the spectator carries all the non-reality. A general vacuum on the line still has a Gibbs-form ascent marginal, with occupation between the two endpoint values, but it entangles the real pair with the spectator, so its ascent mode is purified by the boost qubit and the spectator together. Whether a given inverse temperature, such as $2\pi$, occurs at a point depends on the frame and scale.
synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-re.lay: Two counts of quantum modes appear in the series: modes built from real light-like directions, and the larger number available once complex numbers are allowed. A state described by real numbers alone can only fill the first kind; on the extra mode it is always half full. The pure states that the series attaches to each point of spacetime, its vacua, use the extra mode, so none of them is of that real kind. Writing them out shows that each point's family of vacua is spanned by two special ones. In each of these, provided the point is not on a light ray through the origin, the added direction is entangled only with spacetime's own time-and-space direction and looks thermal on its own, the way half of a pure pair looks hot, while the extra complex mode sits in a fixed state. Mixtures of the two special vacua also look thermal on the added direction, but there the extra mode takes part in the entanglement.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i).} The adjoint extends antilinearly to $\Cl(p,q)_{\C}$, and a state satisfies $\omega(y^{*}) = \overline{\omega(y)}$. synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-.formal:
Let the eight-dimensional Fock module of $\Cl(2,4)$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-real-capacity}, with ground generators $e_{1}$ ($e_{1}^{2} = 1$) and $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ (squares $-1$) and ascent plane $e_{\pm}$ ($e_{\pm}^{2} = \pm 1$), carry that theorem's positive Hermitian structure $h$, for which every generator is unitary. Put $\nO = \tfrac12(e_{+} + e_{-})$, $\ninf = e_{+} - e_{-}$, $X(m) = \nO + m - \tfrac12 Q(m)\ninf$ for $m$ in the complexified span of $e_{1}, \dots, e_{4}$, and let $L(m) \subset \CS$ be the incidence line of $m$, the vacua of $X(m)$ in a chirality half (Proposition \claimref{one-relation.spacetime-manifold-vacuum-lines}). Put $J = i e_{1}e_{+}$ and $\Sigma(\psi, \varphi) = h(\psi, J\varphi)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{($\Sigma$ is the twistor form.)} The positive structure is unique up to a positive factor. $J^{2} = 1$, $J$ is $h$-Hermitian and even, and $\Sigma$ is Hermitian, $\Spin(2,4)$-invariant and of signature $(2,2)$ on each chirality half; on $\CS$ the $\Spin(2,4)$-invariant Hermitian forms are the real multiples of $\Sigma$. So $\Sigma$ is the twistor form of Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor} up to a nonzero real factor.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The positive structure is $\Sigma$ polarised at $\pm i e_{1}$.)} $X(\pm i e_{1}) = e_{+}(1 \mp J)$. Hence $\CS = L(ie_{1}) \oplus L(-ie_{1})$, the two lines are $\Sigma$-orthogonal, and $h = \Sigma$ on $L(ie_{1})$, $h = -\Sigma$ on $L(-ie_{1})$: the positive structure is the twistor form polarised by the incidence lines of the conjugate imaginary points $\pm i e_{1}$, imaginary time one in the units of the Witt pair.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The polarisations are the points of the forward tube.)} The $\Sigma$-adjoint of every real vector is minus itself, so $X(m)^{\sharp} = -X(\bar m)$ and $\Sigma(L(m), L(\bar m)) = 0$ for every complex point $m$. For $m = x + iy$ with $y$ timelike and $y^{1} > 0$, $L(m)$ is $\Sigma$-positive and $L(\bar m)$ is $\Sigma$-negative, so $h_{m} := \Sigma$ on $L(m)$, $-\Sigma$ on $L(\bar m)$, extended $\Sigma$-orthogonally, is a positive Hermitian form on $\CS$ with $h_{m}^{-1}\Sigma$ an involution. Conversely every positive Hermitian form $h'$ on $\CS$ for which $h'^{-1}\Sigma$ is an involution is $h_{m}$ for exactly one such $m$, with the time orientation for which the definite lines of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-the-real-slice}(ii) are positive along $+e_{1}$. The stored structure is $h = h_{ie_{1}}$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Only positive structures carry states.)} Let $s$ be a nondegenerate Hermitian form on a finite-dimensional complex space $V$ and $A \mapsto A^{\sharp}$ its adjoint on $\End(V)$. A linear functional $\omega$ on $\End(V)$ with $\omega(A^{\sharp}A) \ge 0$ for all $A$ and $\omega(1) = 1$ exists if and only if $s$ is definite. So neither $\End(\CS)$ nor the complexified Clifford algebra carries any state for the adjoint of $\Sigma$, and every state of either is a state for a positive Hermitian structure; no positive structure is preserved by a boost, since $(e_{1}e_{2})^{2} = 1$ gives $\exp(\tfrac{\theta}{2}e_{1}e_{2})$ the eigenvalues $e^{\pm\theta/2}$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The centre is the midpoint of the positive half strip.)} Reading Theorem \claimref{synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-the-real-slice}(iii) at $\rho = 1$ with $e_{1}$ as time: along the imaginary boost $x(\theta) = \cos\theta\,e_{2} + i\sin\theta\,e_{1}$ of the real point $e_{2}$ the lines are $\Sigma$-positive for $0 < \theta < \pi$, and at $\theta = \pi/2$ the line is $L(ie_{1})$, the positive part of $h$; for the real point $\rho e_{2}$ the midpoint is $i\rho e_{1}$, the centre of $h$ exactly when $\rho = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-.technical: The open question was whether the selected state reads the positive Hermitian structure, under which every Clifford generator is unitary, or the conformally invariant twistor form, of signature (2,2). They turn out to be one structure. The positive structure equals the twistor form flipped in sign on one of two complementary planes, and those planes are the incidence lines of the complex points plus and minus i times the unit time vector. Every positive structure compatible with the twistor form arises in this way from exactly one complex point whose imaginary part is future timelike, a point of the forward tube (Penrose's classical identification of the positive two-planes of twistor space with the forward tube, re-proved here from the stored statements), and, by a standard Krein-space fact, an algebra whose adjoint comes from an indefinite form has no states at all. So a state must choose a point of the forward tube, and the stored positive structure is the choice of imaginary time one. That point is also the midpoint of the half strip on which an imaginary boost of the unit real point keeps the lines positive (the stored half-strip theorem at unit distance).
synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-.lay: The framework had two candidate ways of measuring the size of quantum states at a point of spacetime: one that treats all directions alike but cannot give every state a positive size, and one that always gives positive sizes but picks out a direction of time and a unit of length. This result shows they are the same thing seen from two places. The positive one is the symmetric one viewed from a particular point of complexified spacetime, one unit along imaginary time, and every positive version of it comes from such a point. Since a quantum state needs positive sizes, a state has to choose such a point; the question of which measure the state uses becomes the question of which point it is viewed from.

\emph{(i)} If $h_{1}, h_{2}$ both make every generator unitary then $h_{1}^{-1}h_{2}$ commutes with the generators, which generate the full matrix algebra of the irreducible module, so it is a scalar; the check confirms that the Hermitian forms for which the six generators are unitary form one real line. $J^{2} = i^{2}e_{1}e_{+}e_{1}e_{+} = -(-e_{1}^{2}e_{+}^{2}) = 1$. $J^{\dagger} = -i\,e_{+}^{\dagger}e_{1}^{\dagger} = -i\,e_{+}e_{1} = i\,e_{1}e_{+} = J$, because $e_{1}, e_{+}$ square to $+1$ and are unitary, hence Hermitian. $J$ is a bivector times $i$, so even, and preserves each chirality half. $\Sigma$ is Hermitian because $J$ is $h$-Hermitian. For a bivector $X = g_{a}g_{b}$, $X^{\dagger} = \epsilon_{a}\epsilon_{b}\,g_{b}g_{a}$ with $\epsilon = +1$ for the Hermitian generators $e_{1}, e_{+}$ and $-1$ for the others, and $J$ commutes with $g_{a}g_{b}$ when $a, b$ are both in $\{e_{1}, e_{+}\}$ or both outside it and anticommutes otherwise; in each case $X^{\dagger}J + JX = 0$, which is $\Spin(2,4)$-invariance of $\Sigma$ (the check verifies all fifteen). On a half $J$ has eigenvalues $+1, +1, -1, -1$ (check), and $h$ is positive, so $\Sigma$ has signature $(2,2)$ there. Uniqueness: an invariant Hermitian form on the irreducible half $\CS$ corresponds to an intertwiner from $\CS$ to the conjugate dual; by Schur these form a space of complex dimension at most one, whose Hermitian elements are a real line. inf$ with $Q(ie_{1}) = -1$, so $X(ie_{1}) = 	frac12(e_{+} + e_{-}) + ie_{1} + 	frac12(e_{+} - e_{-}) = e_{+} + ie_{1}$, and $e_{+}(1 - J) = e_{+} - ie_{+}e_{1}e_{+} = e_{+} + ie_{1}e_{+}^{2} = e_{+} + ie_{1}$. \emph{(iii)} For a generator $g$, $g^{\sharp} = J g^{\dagger}J$ (the $\Sigma$-adjoint, as $J^{-1} = J$ and $J^{\dagger} = J$). The check finds $g^{\sharp} = -g$ for all six; this is the $\Sigma$-anti-Hermiticity of real vectors, of which (i) is the bivector consequence. The adjoint is antilinear in coefficients, so $X(m)^{\sharp} = -X( ar m)$, the coefficients of $

The boost of the $(e_{1}, e_{2})$ plane at imaginary rapidity $i	heta$ sends $e_{2}$ to $\cos	heta\,e_{2} + i\sin	heta\,e_{1}$, with imaginary part $\sin	heta\,e_{1}$, future timelike exactly for $0 < 	heta < \pi$; by (iii) the lines are positive there (the check confirms at $(\cos	heta, \sin	heta) = (\pm	frac35, 	frac45)$ and $(0, 1)$). At $	heta = \pi/2$ the point is $ie_{1}$, whose line is the $+1$ eigenplane of $J$ by (ii). For $ho e_{2}$ the midpoint is $iho e_{1}$, which equals $ie_{1}$ only for $ho = 1$.

\emph{Reading (argued, not part of the statement).} Theorem \claimref{synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-the-real-slice} put the states of the twistor form off the real slice, on the complex points with future timelike imaginary part, and Theorems \claimref{synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-real-capacity} and \claimref{synthesis.boost-stationary-incidence-vacua-read-interval} computed thermal content at real points under the positive structure; the open problem asked which of the two the selected state reads. By (ii) and (iii) the positive structure is the twistor form together with the point $ie_{1}$ of the forward tube, so the second family of results is the first read from that point, and by (iv) a state has to choose such a point. The incidence line of the chosen point is a definite plane, available only off the real slice, which is a complex-capacity object; the marginals at real points are the thermofield doubles of the ascent mode with the boost qubit of the stored synthesis, a real-capacity object. So one state reads both capacities, the complex one through its centre and the real one through its real-point marginals, and the dependence on frame and scale noted in clause (iv) of the thermofield synthesis is the dependence on the tube point. The point $ie_{1}$ is the midpoint of the positive half strip of the imaginary boost of the unit real point, the place a Bisognano-Wichmann-type modular structure would put its vacuum; that identification is not proved here (in the Bisognano-Wichmann picture, cited from memory, vectors are analytic in the imaginary rapidity on the half strip $0 < 	heta < \pi$, half of the KMS strip of width $2\pi$, and the midpoint $	heta = \pi/2$ is where the modular operator enters to the power one quarter; that the time orientation for which $L(ie_{1})$ is positive is the one in which the null translations have positive generator is argued only). Clause (iv) is also a finite-dimensional reason why a boost-KMS state cannot live on the eight-dimensional module: no positive structure there is boost-invariant, so the boost acts unitarily only on a continuum, where the result filed alongside on positive null energy (synthesis.positive-null-energy-gives-r-premises, not yet in the store) poses the corresponding premise and reaches the KMS strip of width $2\pi$, of which the positive half strip $0 < 	heta < \pi$ here is the vector-valued half (the half on which the modular operator enters to the power one half), with midpoint at the power one quarter. The link between the time orientation that makes $L(ie_{1})$ positive and positive null energy is argued, not proved. Nothing here connects the tube point to the selected state of the boundary modes.

synthesis.tube-point-clause-invariant-un.formal:
\emph{The tube-point clause (costed).} Let a state of the series' modes and a wedge with boost $K$ be given, with the compatible tube point $m = x_{\perp} + i\rho u$ over the wedge's bifurcation plane that the boost-KMS data and the ascent pair fix up to the scale $\rho$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.wick-rotated-boost-selects-observer-tube-point}). In a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) of which $K$ generates a symmetry, $m$ is invariant under every symmetry of the field that commutes with $K$, acting on tube points complex-linearly.

\emph{What it is for.} It is the selection rule of the reading of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.de-sitter-field-fixes-the-observer-tube-point}, adopted. In the de Sitter field ($\Lambda > 0$) the symmetries commuting with $K$ are $K$ and a transverse $\so(3)$, and the compatible tube points they fix are exactly one boost orbit, foot at the scale's centre and $\rho^{2} = 12/\Lambda$ (that theorem, (i) and (ii)); so the clause fixes $\rho$ there, and the frozen-point and surface-gravity candidates are one tube point when $\rho = 1/\kappa$ is read as the physical norm of the boost generator (in chart length $\rho_{\Lambda} = 2/\kappa$, the factor $2$ being the local scale $\sigma = 2$). In that field the condition is equivalent to the complexified Stelle-West vector $X(m)/\sigma(m) - \tfrac{3}{\Lambda}I_{\Lambda}$ being purely imaginary (that theorem, (vii)). For the pure-dilation fields with $\Lambda \le 0$ it fixes no tube point and $\rho$ stays free (that theorem, (vi)). It decides fields with one horizon only: in a static region bounded by two horizons it does not say which horizon's boost is the observer's, and the candidates separate there, as in the Schwarzschild-de Sitter field with lapse $f = 1 - 2M/r - \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}r^{2}$ at $\Lambda = M = \tfrac37$, horizons at $r = 1$ and $r = 2$ and $\kappa_{b}/\kappa_{c} = \tfrac85$; for the Schwarzschild field it is not computed. Where it decides, it ties the scale to $\Lambda$ and supplies no unit independent of it.

\emph{What it costs.} It is adopted, not derived from the series' structure. The argument for it runs through the uniqueness of the de Sitter-invariant Hadamard state of a massive scalar (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-hadamard-state-unique}): a state with the symmetry of the field, and a rule assigning tube points covariantly, return a point fixed by the field's symmetries commuting with the boost. The series' boundary modes are CAR fermions, outside that theorem's hypotheses, so the clause carries the hypothesis gap from that theorem to the series' modes. Fields with more than one horizon need a further premise assigning an observer's tube point to one horizon (per observer or per horizon).

\emph{Refutation condition.} The clause is false if any of the following is established: (a) a state of the series' modes on a horizon of the de Sitter field, satisfying the series' other premises, whose compatible tube point is not fixed by the transverse $\so(3)$, for example one whose data fix $\rho^{2} \neq 12/\Lambda$; (b) a derivation from the series' premises of a rule fixing $\rho$ that disagrees with the clause on a field with one horizon; (c) a proof that the series' horizon states on the de Sitter field are not invariant under the field's symmetries commuting with the boost.
synthesis.tube-point-clause-invariant-un.technical: A state of the series reads its capacities at a point of the complexified spacetime, its tube point, which the state's thermal data on a wedge fix up to one scale $\rho$. This clause fixes the scale by symmetry: the tube point must be left in place by every symmetry of the gravitational field that commutes with the wedge's boost. In the de Sitter field those symmetries are the boost and the rotations about the observer, and the only tube points they fix sit at $\rho^{2} = 12/\Lambda$, where the frozen-point and surface-gravity candidates agree as physical lengths. For a vanishing or negative cosmological constant nothing is fixed. The clause is a costed choice: its support is the uniqueness of the symmetric Hadamard state for a massive scalar, which the series' fermionic boundary modes do not satisfy as stated, and it says nothing about which horizon an observer between two horizons belongs to, as in Schwarzschild-de Sitter with surface gravities in the ratio $8/5$. It would be refuted by a series state on de Sitter whose tube point the rotations move, by a derived rule that disagrees with it, or by a proof that the series' horizon states lack the field's symmetry.
synthesis.tube-point-clause-invariant-un.lay: Each observer in this framework is attached to a point of a complexified copy of spacetime, and the framework's thermal data fix that point except for one length. This assumption fixes the length by symmetry: the point must not move under the symmetries of the gravitational field that leave the observer's horizon in place. In a universe with a positive cosmological constant that picks one length, the size set by the cosmological constant; with zero or negative cosmological constant it picks none, and with two horizons it cannot say which horizon counts. It is adopted with these limits stated, and could be overturned by a calculation or derivation that disagrees with it.

synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-t.technical:
The positive Hermitian structure under which the incidence vacua were found to be thermofield doubles is not invariant under the conformal group. The store also has an invariant structure, the twistor form $\Sigma$ of signature $(2,2)$, under which the lines of real points are exactly the $\Sigma$-null lines. Restricting $\Sigma$ to the line of a complex point $x + iy$ gives $-2$ times the Hermitian form of the imaginary part $y$, whose determinant has the sign of $Q(y)$: null for real points, definite for timelike $y$, split for spacelike $y$, degenerate for null $y$. This is the classical correspondence between the halves of twistor space and the forward and backward tubes. Computed on the stored construction itself, the definite lines are positive when $y$ points along $+e_{0}$.

Along an imaginary boost of a point of the right wedge, $x(\theta) = \rho\cos\theta\,e_{1} + i\rho\sin\theta\,e_{0}$, the line is definite of opposite signs on the two half strips and null at $0$ and $\pi$, where the point is real again and reflected; for the stored $\kappa$ the restricted form is $2\rho\sin\theta$ times a fixed positive form, positive on $0 < \theta < \pi$. So with the invariant structure, real spacetime is pure geometry, a family of null lines saturating the form's isotropic dimension, and states exist only on the complex continuation, on one half strip of the rapidity period $2\pi$.
synthesis.twistor-form-states-only-off-t.lay: Earlier work found that, at each point of spacetime, the series' quantum vacua include thermal states, but it used a way of measuring states that does not respect the symmetries of spacetime. This result redoes the analysis with the measure that does respect them. Then every real point of spacetime corresponds to a family of vacua of zero norm, pure geometry with no states on it; genuine states appear only when the point is continued into complex values. Along that continuation the states exist for exactly half of one full turn. A suggested reading, not proved here, is that this half-turn matches the half period that appears in the imaginary-time treatment of Hawking's temperature.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} By Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(2)-(4), $\Sigma$ is a Hermitian form on $\CS$ of signature $(2,2)$ for which $\Som$ and $\Spi$ are null, and by (5) $\sigma = \Sigma|_{\Som\times\Spi}$ is a perfect pairing and the real points of the chart of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart} are exactly $A = i\hat x$ with $\hat x$ $\sigma$-Hermitian, $i$ the complex unit of the Fock model (which acts as $I_{6}$ up to sign). The chart map is complex linear (Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart}(2)), so the complex point $x + iy$ has $A = i\hat x + i(i\hat y) = i\hat x - \hat y$.

\emph{(i)} For $Z = A\pi + \pi$ and $Z' = A\pi' + \pi'$, nullity of the halves and hermiticity give $\Sigma(Z, Z') = \sigma(A\pi, \pi') + \overline{\sigma(A\pi', \pi)}$. With $\sigma$ antilinear in its first slot and $\hat x$, $\hat y$ $\sigma$-Hermitian, the terms in $i\hat x$ give $-i\sigma(\hat x\pi,\pi') + \overline{-i\sigma(\hat x\pi',\pi)} = -i\sigma(\hat x\pi,\pi') + i\sigma(\hat x\pi,\pi') = 0$, and the terms in $-\hat y$ give $-\sigma(\hat y\pi,\pi') - \overline{\sigma(\hat y\pi',\pi)} = -2\sigma(\hat y\pi,\pi')$. So $\Sigma|_{L} = -2\,\sigma(\hat y\,\cdot,\cdot)$, which depends on $y$ only. In bases of $\Som$, $\Spi$ dual for $\sigma$ the form $\sigma(\hat y\,\cdot,\cdot)$ is a Hermitian matrix $Y$, and by clause (5) of the Proposition its determinant is a positive multiple of $Q(y)$ (the chart norm on real points is $2\det\hat x$); a change of basis of $L$ multiplies the determinant by a positive number, so the sign of $\det(\Sigma|_{L})$ is the sign of $Q(y)$.

\emph{The check computes all of this on the stored construction.} It rebuilds the Fock model, the Chevalley pairing, the real orthonormal basis $a_{1}, a_{2}, b_{1}, \dots, b_{4}$ with $w_{3} = b_{3} + ib_{4}$, $\kappa = \Gamma C(b_{4})J$ and $\Sigma = \mu B(\kappa\,\cdot,\cdot)$ exactly as the stored Proposition defines them (with $c = \sqrt{2}C$, a positive rescaling, and the stored phase, here $\lambda = 1$, $\mu = 2$), and the stored chart (the graph line in the stored bases $\pi_{1}, \pi_{2}, e_{1}, e_{2}$, with $m(A)$ read through the spinor identification). It checks that $\Sigma$ is Hermitian of rank four with both halves null and $\kappa^{2} < 0$, that the chart reproduces the four basis vectors $e_{0} = a_{2}$, $e_{1} = b_{2}$, $e_{2} = b_{3}$, $e_{3} = b_{4}$ of the Minkowski complement, and that the lines of real points are $\Sigma$-null. For six imaginary parts $y$ (timelike of both orientations, spacelike, null) and two real parts it finds the Gram matrix of $\Sigma$ on the line, in the basis $(A\pi_{1} + \pi_{1}, A\pi_{2} + \pi_{2})$, independent of $x$, with determinant $4Q(y)$ and trace $4y^{0}$.

\emph{(ii)} A Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrix is definite iff its determinant is positive, then with the sign of its trace; split iff its determinant is negative; and of rank one iff its determinant vanishes and it is nonzero. With determinant $4Q(y)$ and trace $4y^{0}$ this gives the four cases, the definite lines being positive exactly when $y^{0} > 0$. This sign is a property of the stored $\kappa$ and of the orientation of $e_{0}$: replacing $\kappa$ by $-\kappa$ replaces $\Sigma$ by $-\Sigma$, and reversing $e_{0}$ reverses $y^{0}$; either exchanges the two orientations. (A simplified model with $\Sigma = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and the Pauli assignment $\hat y(e_{0}) = +1$ gives the opposite sign, which is why the sign is computed on the stored construction.)

\emph{(iii)} The boost of the $(e_{0}, e_{1})$ plane with rapidity $\lambda$ sends $te_{0} + re_{1}$ to $(t\cosh\lambda + r\sinh\lambda)e_{0} + (t\sinh\lambda + r\cosh\lambda)e_{1}$; at $\lambda = i\theta$ and $(t, r) = (0, \rho)$ this is $\rho\cos\theta\,e_{1} + i\rho\sin\theta\,e_{0}$, with $Q(y) = \rho^{2}\sin^{2}\theta$ and $y^{0} = \rho\sin\theta$. The check finds the Gram matrix $2\rho\sin\theta$ times the identity at the Pythagorean angles $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) = (\pm\tfrac35, \pm\tfrac45)$ and at $\theta = 0, \pi$ (with $\rho = \tfrac32$): positive for $0 < \theta < \pi$, negative for $\pi < \theta < 2\pi$, zero at $\theta \in \{0, \pi\}$, where $x(0) = x_{0}$ and $x(\pi) = -x_{0}$ are real. The orbit is $2\pi$-periodic since $x(\theta)$ depends on $\theta$ through $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$.

\emph{Reading.} The positive Hermitian structure of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.incidence-vacua-thermofield-real-capacity} is not $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$-invariant (its clause (iv)); $\Sigma$ is (Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(2)). Under $\Sigma$, by (ii), no line of a real point carries a positive state; the incidence line of a real point is a maximal isotropic plane for a form of Witt index two, a real-capacity count for $\Sigma$ in the sense of Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences}. By (iii) positivity along an imaginary boost holds on exactly one half strip, $0 < \theta < \pi$ for the stored $\kappa$ and imaginary part along $+e_{0}$.

synthesis.wick-rotated-boost-selects-obs.technical: The previous result showed that a state on the conformal spinor module must choose a point of the forward tube, the choice fixing the positive Hermitian structure. Here the choice is tied to a wedge and its boost. The tube points whose positive structure makes the imaginary-rapidity (Wick-rotated) boost a unitary symmetry are exactly the complex points whose real part lies on the bifurcation plane and whose imaginary part is a future timelike vector of the boost plane; they are also the points fixed by the antiholomorphic wedge reflection, the geometric form of a modular conjugation. Each lies a quarter turn of the Wick-rotated boost from a single real point of the wedge: its imaginary part is the distance of that point from the bifurcation plane times the unit tangent of the boost orbit through it. The Wick-rotated boost has weights one half and changes sign at a full turn. Finally, an ascent mode based at a point of the bifurcation plane is invariant under the boost, so any state KMS for the boost gives it occupation one half. Its number operator is Hermitian for the positive structure only when the tube point stands over that base point, and for an observer standing over it, and only at the observer's own tube point, every vacuum of the incidence line has occupation one half, so the line is compatible with the boost-KMS state whichever vacuum is taken, and its thermofield doubles become maximally entangled pairs of the ascent mode with the boost qubit. So the ascent pair fixes the foot on the bifurcation plane; the scale, the distance from that plane, is the one datum the boost and KMS data leave free.
synthesis.wick-rotated-boost-selects-obs.lay: An earlier result showed that a quantum state at a point of this geometry has to pick a point of a complexified spacetime, and that this choice sets how sizes of states are measured. This result asks which point a state of the kind the series uses, thermal for the boost of one horizon wedge, would pick. The compatible points sit directly over the horizon's two-dimensional edge, displaced into imaginary time, and each corresponds to exactly one observer outside the horizon: rotating that observer a quarter turn in imaginary time lands on it, and how far into imaginary time it sits is the observer's distance from the horizon's edge. The mode in question is tied to one point of the edge. For an observer standing over that point, and only at that observer's own complex point, the description of the point as a line of possible vacuum states agrees in full with what thermality for the boost demands of the mode: it is exactly half filled, fully entangled with the boost's own qubit. So where along the edge is fixed; what remains free is how far from it.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting and two preliminary facts.} Everything is in the module and with the notation of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}; the check realises it as three fermionic modes in the Jordan-Wigner basis over the Gaussian rationals. Write $A^{\sharp}$ for the $\Sigma$-adjoint. By (iii) of that theorem every real vector is $\Sigma$-anti-Hermitian, so for the real bivector $e_{1}e_{2}$, $(e_{1}e_{2})^{\sharp} = e_{2}^{\sharp}e_{1}^{\sharp} = e_{2}e_{1} = -e_{1}e_{2}$, and $K^{\sharp} = -K$. Write $J_{m}$ for the involution equal to $+1$ on $L(m)$ and $-1$ on $L( ar m)$, so that $h_{m} = \Sigma(\cdot, J_{m}\cdot)$; the $h_{m}$-adjoint is $A^{\dagger_{m}} = J_{m}A^{\sharp}J_{m}$.

Two features of such a state have finite-dimensional images here. Its Euclidean continuation is a rotation in imaginary rapidity, and in the Osterwalder-Schrader picture (cited from memory) that rotation is a symmetry of the Euclidean structure, which is condition (i) on the positive structure; and in the Bisognano-Wichmann theorem (cited from memory) the wedge vacuum's modular conjugation is the wedge reflection, whose fixed set is the same family.
